solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Interruption from Asquith, ignoring question rudely

indicators.note: the question is left out of the letters used
the letters are handled roughly, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: the name supplies the fodder
Q = question, dropped from ASQUITH

explanation.surface: A heckler interrupts the Edwardian prime minister Asquith, brushing aside a question.
explanation.walkthrough: Asquith is used purely for his letters; take out Q and the six left rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiatus is a gap or break, an interruption in continuity.

clue.text: Tall story capturing female's extravagant ways

parts.note: tall = high

indicators.note: the story holds the female inside it

parts.note: a story = a lie
F = female, captured inside LIE

explanation.surface: A tall tale about some woman's lavish lifestyle.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tall story" reads as one phrase meaning a fib, but the two words do separate jobs, and the female sits inside the story.
explanation.definitionFit: The high life is a lavish, extravagant way of living.

clue.text: A different answer by a different lady?

parts.note: A = answer
a different lady is NOT HER

explanation.surface: A riddle about a second answer supplied by some second woman.
explanation.walkthrough: "Different" appears twice on purpose: the first time it belongs to the definition, the second to a lady who is "not her".
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the answer stands for "a different one", as in try another road.

clue.text: You uttered sense about tangled vine, not green?

indicators.note: the sense goes round the vine

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced you

indicators.note: the vine's letters are twisted up

parts.note: nous = common sense
VINE rearranged, set inside NOUS

explanation.surface: Someone with good sense disentangles a vine that is no longer green.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that "green" means envious, not the colour of a leaf, which the vine invites.
explanation.definitionFit: Green is envy's colour, so someone not green is unenvious.

clue.text: Short of energy, recommend drinking a sugary drink

indicators.note: the word lacks the energy letter
the word takes the A inside it

parts.note: to advocate = to recommend
E = energy, removed from the end: ADVOCAT
the letter A, drunk by what is left of the word, just before its last two letters

explanation.surface: A tired adviser suggests a sweet drink to perk up.
explanation.walkthrough: ADVOCAAT is a Dutch egg-and-brandy liqueur; after dropping E, the A slips in before the final AT.
explanation.definitionFit: Advocaat is a sweet, thick liqueur made with eggs, sugar and brandy.

clue.text: Some dialogue in winter time, as well as preceding period in US novel

parts.note: Dec = December
a line is a piece of dialogue
as well as = and
fall is the American autumn, the season before winter

explanation.surface: Someone reads lines of a winter-set American novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel is Evelyn Waugh's; "in US" belongs to FALL, not to the novel, which is British.
explanation.definitionFit: Decline and Fall is Evelyn Waugh's first novel (1928).

clue.text: Admit I'm hurt over witticism taken the wrong way

parts.note: ow! is what you say when hurt

indicators.note: the witticism is read backwards

parts.note: a pun is a witticism, turned round to NUP

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they were wounded by a joke they misunderstood.
explanation.walkthrough: "Taken the wrong way" sounds like offence taken; here it just means reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to confess a fault is to admit it.

clue.text: Source of music containing a boring song in idyllic setting

indicators.note: the source of music holds the A

parts.note: an aria is an operatic song

indicators.note: the result drills into the song

parts.note: a CD is a source of music
A goes inside CD, making CAD, which bores into ARIA

explanation.surface: Music drifts over a pastoral scene, even if the song is a dull one.
explanation.walkthrough: "A boring song" looks like a dull tune; "boring" is the instruction that CAD goes inside ARIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcadia is the idealised rural paradise of pastoral poetry.

clue.text: In essay, absorbing conclusion

indicators.note: the essay takes the conclusion inside it

parts.note: an essay is an attempt, a try
conclusion = end

explanation.surface: An essay that takes in its conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: "In" looks like a mere preposition, but it is the definition, meaning fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: "in" as an adjective means currently fashionable.

clue.text: Nice bar Corelli composed is utterly resistant to harmonisation

indicators.note: the letters are put together afresh

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A charming bar of music written by the baroque composer Corelli simply will not take harmony.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface makes "composed" and "harmonisation" look literal; one shuffles letters and the other belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Things irreconcilable cannot be brought into agreement.

clue.text: Kind of mean old setter stopping to make a fortune, almost

indicators.note: the phrase loses its last letter
the pair plugs a gap inside the phrase

parts.note: GET RICH without its final H; OME stops the gap
O = old
the setter refers to themself as ME

explanation.surface: A stingy old crossword setter stops just short of getting rich.
explanation.walkthrough: "Mean" pulls towards stinginess, which the old setter supports; it is the mathematical average.
explanation.definitionFit: The geometric mean is one kind of average, alongside the arithmetic mean.

clue.text: Seaside resort around west end of Hudson Bay

indicators.note: the resort surrounds the letter

parts.note: Nice is a resort on the French Riviera

indicators.note: in an across clue the west end is the first letter

parts.note: first letter of Hudson

explanation.surface: A seaside resort somewhere near Hudson Bay in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: "Hudson Bay" is a geographic unit in the surface; split it, and Bay alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bay is a recess in a wall, the same thing as a niche.

clue.text: Composer's right tucking into case of vintage port

indicators.note: to tuck into something is to get inside it

parts.note: LEHAR, the operetta composer, whose final letter is his right (R), moved below

indicators.note: the outer letters of vintage

parts.note: outer letters of vintage, with R tucked inside
R = right, the last letter of LEHAR

explanation.surface: A composer tucks into a bottle of vintage port.
explanation.walkthrough: Franz Lehar wrote The Merry Widow. His name ends in R, the right, and that R tucks into VE; "port" looks like the wine but is the town.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Havre is a major French seaport on the Seine estuary.

clue.text: Prevented rogue journalist inhibiting second one

parts.note: an imp is a little rogue
ED = editor
a second journalist, another ED

explanation.surface: A rogue reporter holds back a colleague from doing something.
explanation.walkthrough: "Inhibiting" works as a restraint in the surface; the first ED holds the second one back behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: To impede is to hinder or prevent, so impeded = prevented.

clue.text: Undertake long journey cycling in US city

indicators.note: the last part moves round to the front

parts.note: to go far is to travel a long way; GO moves to the end

explanation.surface: A long bike ride through an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cycling" suggests a bike tour; here it rotates GO FAR into FARGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Fargo is the largest city in North Dakota.

clue.text: Are greedy banks hard to stimulate excessively?

parts.note: those who overeat are greedy
H = hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A jibe at greedy banks for overheating the economy.
explanation.walkthrough: "Banks" looks like financial institutions; it is a verb, OVEREAT flanking H.
explanation.definitionFit: To overheat an economy or engine is to stimulate it too much.

clue.text: Time after a match away from home?

definitions.text: Time after a match away from home?

parts.note: surface reading: the spell after a football game; meant: the spell after a wedding, a match between two people
surface reading: an away fixture; meant: a holiday the newlyweds take away from home

explanation.surface: A footballer's schedule after an away fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: "Match" sounds like sport and "away from home" like an away game; the match is a marriage and the time away is the holiday after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A honeymoon is the holiday newlyweds take after the wedding.

clue.text: Maybe chop chop with these tips for minimising expenses and charges

indicators.note: the first letters of the next three words

parts.note: first letters of minimising, expenses, and
taxes are charges

explanation.surface: A finance guru offers speedy tips for cutting costs and charges.
explanation.walkthrough: "Chop chop" reads as hurry up; here it is a chop of meat being chopped. Note that "and" is used twice, once as fodder and once to join.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat axes, or cleavers, are what you chop a pork chop with.

clue.text: Perhaps "Napoleon" is deliberately written thus in my article

parts.note: cor! and my! are both exclamations of surprise
sic marks a quoted error as intentional
an = indefinite article

explanation.surface: An editor's note that a name has been spelt that way on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: "My" is the exclamation, not the possessive; cor is British slang for the same surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon was born on Corsica, so he is one example of a Corsican.

clue.text: Not even a tech giant provides opportunities for factotum

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd
Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple

explanation.surface: Not even a big tech firm is creating jobs for handymen.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tech giant" invites a company name; it is a person, Steve Jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A factotum is a do-anything helper, whose work is odd jobs.

clue.text: New decoration absorbing fifty grand

parts.note: N = new

indicators.note: the decoration takes the fifty inside it

parts.note: OBE, the British honour Order of the British Empire
L = 50 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A newly decorated person picks up fifty thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: "Grand" invites a thousand pounds after fifty; it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Noble and grand both mean stately or magnificent.

clue.text: Beginning to bluster and blither, one's prickly

definitions.note: "One's prickly" means "one that is prickly", a noun phrase

indicators.note: take the first letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of bluster
to blither is to talk aimlessly, to ramble

explanation.surface: Someone blusters and blathers, which makes them touchy.
explanation.walkthrough: "Prickly" reads as bad-tempered, matching the blusterer; the definition is a thorny plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A bramble is a thorny blackberry bush, a prickly one.

clue.text: Word used in footnoting current book doctor cut up

indicators.note: the doctor loses his last letter

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
B = book

indicators.note: in a down clue, the letters read upwards

parts.note: a medic is a doctor; cut to MEDI, then reversed

explanation.surface: A footnote about a book on current affairs that a doctor tore apart.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cut up" looks like one phrase meaning chopped or upset; it is two instructions, trim and reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibidem, abbreviated ibid., means "in the same place" in footnotes.

clue.text: Harry is immoral, following socialite around

indicators.note: the socialite is turned round
the immoral part comes after

parts.note: a deb (debutante) is a young socialite
immoral = evil

explanation.surface: Prince Harry is a scoundrel, chasing after a society girl.
explanation.walkthrough: "Harry" is a verb here, to harass, not the prince.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry is to torment persistently, the same as to bedevil.

clue.text: Flipping unwell? I see it's parts of the intestines

indicators.note: the whole string is turned over

parts.note: unwell = ill
I as printed
V is short for vide, Latin for see; ILLIV then reads backwards

explanation.surface: Someone feeling rotten realises it is their gut.
explanation.walkthrough: "Flipping" looks like a mild British swearword; it is the instruction to reverse ILL + I + V.
explanation.definitionFit: Villi are the tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine.

clue.text: Shrewd way to maintain yearly spectacle for Sky viewer

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or shrewd
p.a. = per annum
St = street

explanation.surface: A satellite TV subscriber finds a smart way to keep their annual viewing going.
explanation.walkthrough: "Sky" is capitalised to suggest the British broadcaster Sky; the viewer is simply looking at the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: A fly-past is a ceremonial flight of aircraft, watched from the ground.

clue.text: Rascal's opening toy boxes, provoking a wry smile

indicators.note: the toy encloses that letter

parts.note: a doll is a toy

indicators.note: the first letter of Rascal

parts.note: first letter of Rascal, boxed in DOLL

explanation.surface: A cheeky child opens the toy box, which raises a knowing smile.
explanation.walkthrough: "Toy boxes" reads as a noun, a toy box; "boxes" is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Droll means amusing in a dry, odd way, so provoking a wry smile.

clue.text: Pass back to part of pitch into which crosses go?

indicators.note: the word is written backwards

parts.note: in football, a ball is a pass
TO turned back
the penalty box on a football pitch

explanation.surface: A footballer passes back towards the penalty area, where crosses land.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is football, so crosses seem to be balls into the box; they are the X marks voters make.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters mark their ballot paper with a cross and post it into the ballot box.

clue.text: French scorer and World Cup winner Bayern regularly snubbed

parts.note: Lionel Messi, captain of Argentina's 2022 winners

indicators.note: every other letter is ignored

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of Bayern

explanation.surface: A French goalscorer, a World Cup winner and the club Bayern Munich all get a mention.
explanation.walkthrough: "Scorer" means someone who writes musical scores: Olivier Messiaen, the French composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Messiaen was a 20th-century French composer, and composers write scores.

clue.text: Thinker Friedrich Nietzsche, returning drained, begins to work

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so the two letters read in reverse
emptied of its middle, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: outer letters of Nietzsche, reversed to EN
a plan gels when it starts to come together

explanation.surface: The philosopher Nietzsche, exhausted, gets back to his work.
explanation.walkthrough: Both thinkers are called Friedrich, so the surface steers to Nietzsche; the answer is Friedrich Engels, Marx's collaborator.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Engels was the German philosopher who co-wrote The Communist Manifesto.
